claim: TAPBPR is a peptide exchange catalyst that is important for optimal peptide selection by MHC class I molecules.
source: Recently, we revealed that TAPBPR is a peptide exchange catalyst that is important for optimal peptide selection by MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references the authors' previous work.

claim: TAPBPR interacts with UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1).
source: We identify an interaction between TAPBPR and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1), a folding sensor in the calnexin/calreticulin quality control cycle that is known to regenerate the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety on glycoproteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: UGT1 is a folding sensor in the calnexin/calreticulin quality control cycle.
source: We identify an interaction between TAPBPR and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1), a folding sensor in the calnexin/calreticulin quality control cycle that is known to regenerate the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety on glycoproteins.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about UGT1's function.

claim: UGT1 regenerates the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety on glycoproteins.
source: We identify an interaction between TAPBPR and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1), a folding sensor in the calnexin/calreticulin quality control cycle that is known to regenerate the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety on glycoproteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UGT1's enzymatic function.

claim: A multimeric complex forms between TAPBPR, UGT1, and MHC class I molecules.
source: Our results suggest the formation of a multimeric complex, dependent on a conserved cysteine at position 94 in TAPBPR, in which TAPBPR promotes the association of UGT1 with peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The formation of the TAPBPR-UGT1-MHC class I complex is dependent on a conserved cysteine at position 94 in TAPBPR.
source: Our results suggest the formation of a multimeric complex, dependent on a conserved cysteine at position 94 in TAPBPR, in which TAPBPR promotes the association of UGT1 with peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3A and Table 2.

claim: TAPBPR promotes the association of UGT1 with peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules.
source: Our results suggest the formation of a multimeric complex, dependent on a conserved cysteine at position 94 in TAPBPR, in which TAPBPR promotes the association of UGT1 with peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The interaction between TAPBPR and UGT1 facilitates the reglucosylation of the glycan on MHC class I molecules.
source: We reveal that the interaction between TAPBPR and UGT1 facilities the reglucosylation of the glycan on MHC class I molecules, promoting their recognition by calreticulin.
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Reglucosylation of MHC class I molecules by the TAPBPR-UGT1 complex promotes their recognition by calreticulin.
source: We reveal that the interaction between TAPBPR and UGT1 facilities the reglucosylation of the glycan on MHC class I molecules, promoting their recognition by calreticulin.
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TAPBPR improves peptide optimisation by promoting peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules to associate with the peptide-loading complex.
source: Our results suggest that in addition to being a peptide editor, TAPBPR improves peptide optimisation by promoting peptide-receptive MHC class I molecules to associate with the peptide-loading complex.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing increased association of MHC class I with tapasin and TAP in cells expressing TAPBPR wild-type versus C94A mutant (Figure 6B).

claim: Tapasin functions as a peptide exchange catalyst for MHC class I molecules.
source: It is now well established that tapasin functions as a peptide exchange catalyst for MHC class I molecules, a process that is important in the selection of high-affinity peptides onto MHC class I molecules (Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TAPBPR functions as a peptide exchange catalyst for MHC class I molecules.
source: Recently, we revealed that TAPBPR, a second MHC class I-dedicated chaperone in the antigen presentation pathway, also functions as a peptide exchange catalyst for MHC class I molecules (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015), a finding that was subsequently verified by Margulies and colleagues (Morozov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work and independent verification.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR cannot directly compensate for each other within a cellular environment.
source: Although both tapasin and TAPBPR share the ability to optimise peptide selection in vitro, they cannot directly compensate for each other within a cellular environment and appear to influence peptide selection in separate yet complementary processes.
evidence: This is based on the authors' interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR influence peptide selection in separate yet complementary processes.
source: Although both tapasin and TAPBPR share the ability to optimise peptide selection in vitro, they cannot directly compensate for each other within a cellular environment and appear to influence peptide selection in separate yet complementary processes.
evidence: This is based on the authors' interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: In the absence of tapasin, inefficient peptide loading occurs, resulting in MHC class I molecules loaded with suboptimal peptide ligands.
source: In the absence of a functional tapasin molecule, inefficient peptide loading occurs, resulting in MHC class I molecules loaded with suboptimal peptide ligands (Ortmann et al., 1997; Purcell et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The absence of tapasin produces thermolabile MHC class I complexes that are inefficiently expressed on the cell surface.
source: As a consequence, the absence of tapasin produces thermolabile MHC class I complexes that are inefficiently expressed on the cell surface, although different MHC class I allomorphs differ in their dependency on tapasin (Ortmann et al., 1997; Lewis et al., 1998; Peh et al., 1998; Garbi et al., 2000; Grandea et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2002; Rizvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Different MHC class I allomorphs differ in their dependency on tapasin.
source: As a consequence, the absence of tapasin produces thermolabile MHC class I complexes that are inefficiently expressed on the cell surface, although different MHC class I allomorphs differ in their dependency on tapasin (Ortmann et al., 1997; Lewis et al., 1998; Peh et al., 1998; Garbi et al., 2000; Grandea et al., 2000; Williams et al., 2002; Rizvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TAPBPR is not essential for the initial peptide-loading event onto MHC class I molecules.
source: TAPBPR is not essential for the initial peptide-loading event onto MHC class I molecules (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TAPBPR has a fine-tuning effect on the peptides displayed, removing some peptides of lower affinity and thus improving peptide selection and increasing the stability of MHC class I molecules.
source: Instead, TAPBPR has a more subtle, fine-tuning effect on the peptides displayed, removing some peptides of lower affinity and thus improving peptide selection and increasing the stability of MHC class I molecules (Hermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Tapasin functions within the peptide-loading complex in an environment that is rich in suitable peptides for MHC class I binding.
source: Tapasin functions within the PLC in an environment that is rich in suitable peptides for MHC class I binding (Sadasivan et al., 1996; Li et al., 1997; Ortmann et al., 1997), which helps promote efficient peptide loading onto MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TAPBPR is not a component of the peptide-loading complex.
source: In contrast TAPBPR is not a component of the PLC and therefore performs peptide editing outside this complex, potentially in a more peptide-deficient environment (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015), which may favour peptide dissociation from MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TAPBPR performs peptide editing outside the peptide-loading complex, potentially in a more peptide-deficient environment.
source: In contrast TAPBPR is not a component of the PLC and therefore performs peptide editing outside this complex, potentially in a more peptide-deficient environment (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015), which may favour peptide dissociation from MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is supported by citations and speculation about the functional environment.

claim: The transmembrane domain of tapasin is responsible for its interaction with TAP.
source: For tapasin, three regions have been identified that are essential for its localisation and function within the PLC: its transmembrane domain is responsible for its interaction with TAP (Petersen et al., 2005; Rufer et al., 2015);
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A free cysteine residue at position C95 in tapasin is essential for its association with ERp57.
source: a free cysteine residue at position C95 is essential for its association with ERp57 (Dick et al., 2002; Peaper et al., 2005);
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Residues in the Ig domains of tapasin interact with MHC class I.
source: and residues in the Ig domains interact with MHC class I (Turnquist et al., 2001; Turnquist et al., 2004, Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: UGT1 was identified in the immunoprecipitate from ZZ-TAPBPR-expressing cells but not in control cells.
source: Interestingly, UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1) was also isolated in the immunoprecipitates from ZZ-TAPBPR-expressing cells, but not in control HeLaM cells transfected with an empty vector (Table 1), suggesting that UGT1 could be a novel binding partner for TAPBPR.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: UGT1 was ranked as the third specific hit in the ZZ-TAPBPR pulldown after the MHC class I heavy chain and TAPBPR.
source: UGT1 was ranked as the third specific hit in the ZZ-TAPBPR pulldown after the MHC class I heavy chain and TAPBPR (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: UGT1 is an ER/cis-Golgi resident enzyme that monitors glycoprotein folding.
source: UGT1 is an ER/cis-Golgi resident enzyme that monitors glycoprotein folding (Arnold et al., 2000; Tessier et al., 2000; Zuber et al., 2001; D'Alessio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: UGT1 plays an important role in the MHC class I antigen processing and presentation pathway.
source: In 2011, Cresswell and colleagues showed that UGT1 plays an important role in the MHC class I antigen processing and presentation pathway (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In UGT1-deficient cells, MHC class I maturation and assembly was delayed, surface expression of MHC class I was reduced, and there was an impairment of peptide selection.
source: Although no direct association was demonstrated between MHC class I and UGT1 within a cellular environment, they found that MHC class I maturation and assembly was delayed, surface expression of MHC class I was reduced, and there was an impairment of peptide selection in UGT1-deficient cells (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Recombinant UGT1 reglucosylates MHC class I molecules associated with suboptimal ligands and permits their re-engagement with the peptide-loading complex.
source: Furthermore, recombinant UGT1 was found to reglucosylate MHC class I molecules associated with suboptimal ligands and permitted their re-engagement with the PLC, thus providing direct evidence for the role of UGT1 in the antigen presentation pathway (Wearsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: An association between endogenous TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in IFN-γ-treated HeLaM cells.
source: An association between endogenous TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in both IFN-γ-treated HeLaM and KBM-7 cells (Figure 1A and B respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An association between endogenous TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in IFN-γ-treated KBM-7 cells.
source: An association between endogenous TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in both IFN-γ-treated HeLaM and KBM-7 cells (Figure 1A and B respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The co-precipitation of UGT1 was not observed in cells that were knocked out or depleted of TAPBPR.
source: The association was not observed in cells that were knocked out (Figure 1A) or depleted (Figure 1B) of TAPBPR, demonstrating that the co-precipitation of UGT1 was a direct consequence of TAPBPR presence.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The association between TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in the absence of tapasin.
source: Furthermore, the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in the absence of tapasin (Figure 1A and B), suggesting that a functional PLC is not required for TAPBPR to associate with UGT1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: A functional peptide-loading complex is not required for TAPBPR to associate with UGT1.
source: Furthermore, the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 was observed in the absence of tapasin (Figure 1A and B), suggesting that a functional PLC is not required for TAPBPR to associate with UGT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TAPBPR-UGT1 association occurs in tapasin knockout cells.

claim: The association between TAPBPR and MHC class I was increased in the absence of tapasin.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B, we observed that the association between TAPBPR and MHC class I was increased in the absence of tapasin, an observation that is consistent with our previously published findings (Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1A and 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: No association was observed between tapasin and UGT1 in IFN-γ-induced KBM-7 cells.
source: In contrast to the association observed between TAPBPR and UGT1, no association was observed between tapasin and UGT1 in IFN-γ-induced KBM-7 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Human TAPBPR lacks an N-linked glycan.
source: However, as human TAPBPR lacks an N-linked glycan and UGT1 monitors glycoprotein folding by recognising hydrophobic patches near a Man9GlcNAc2 moiety (Trombetta et al., 1989; Caramelo et al., 2003, Caramelo et al., 2004; Ritter et al., 2005), it is highly unlikely that UGT1 functions directly in the quality control of TAPBPR.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of TAPBPR structure.

claim: UGT1 monitors glycoprotein folding by recognising hydrophobic patches near a Man9GlcNAc2 moiety.
source: However, as human TAPBPR lacks an N-linked glycan and UGT1 monitors glycoprotein folding by recognising hydrophobic patches near a Man9GlcNAc2 moiety (Trombetta et al., 1989; Caramelo et al., 2003, Caramelo et al., 2004; Ritter et al., 2005), it is highly unlikely that UGT1 functions directly in the quality control of TAPBPR.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It is highly unlikely that UGT1 functions directly in the quality control of TAPBPR.
source: However, as human TAPBPR lacks an N-linked glycan and UGT1 monitors glycoprotein folding by recognising hydrophobic patches near a Man9GlcNAc2 moiety (Trombetta et al., 1989; Caramelo et al., 2003, Caramelo et al., 2004; Ritter et al., 2005), it is highly unlikely that UGT1 functions directly in the quality control of TAPBPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that TAPBPR lacks an N-linked glycan, which is required for UGT1 recognition.

claim: Intramolecular disulphide bonds exist between C7 and C71 in the N-terminal domain of tapasin.
source: For tapasin, intramolecular disulphide bonds exist between C7 and C71 in the N-terminal domain and C295 and C363 in the membrane proximal Ig-like domain, while C95 is known not to be involved in an intramolecular disulphide bound, but instead forms an intermolecular disulphide bond with C57 of ERp57 (Herberg et al., 1998; Dick et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2009)(Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intramolecular disulphide bonds exist between C295 and C363 in the membrane proximal Ig-like domain of tapasin.
source: For tapasin, intramolecular disulphide bonds exist between C7 and C71 in the N-terminal domain and C295 and C363 in the membrane proximal Ig-like domain, while C95 is known not to be involved in an intramolecular disulphide bound, but instead forms an intermolecular disulphide bond with C57 of ERp57 (Herberg et al., 1998; Dick et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2009)(Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C95 in tapasin forms an intermolecular disulphide bond with C57 of ERp57.
source: For tapasin, intramolecular disulphide bonds exist between C7 and C71 in the N-terminal domain and C295 and C363 in the membrane proximal Ig-like domain, while C95 is known not to be involved in an intramolecular disulphide bound, but instead forms an intermolecular disulphide bond with C57 of ERp57 (Herberg et al., 1998; Dick et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2009)(Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C18 and C101 in the N-terminal domain of TAPBPR form intramolecular disulphide bonds.
source: Our Fold and Functional Assignment System (FFAS) model of TAPBPR (Hermann et al., 2013) now supported by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data (Morozov et al., 2016), predicts that C18 and C101 in the N-terminal domain and C300 and C361 in the IgC domain of TAPBPR form similar intramolecular disulphide bonds as those found in tapasin, and that C191 and C262 form an additional intramolecular disulphide bond (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is predicted by structural modeling and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C300 and C361 in the IgC domain of TAPBPR form intramolecular disulphide bonds.
source: Our Fold and Functional Assignment System (FFAS) model of TAPBPR (Hermann et al., 2013) now supported by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data (Morozov et al., 2016), predicts that C18 and C101 in the N-terminal domain and C300 and C361 in the IgC domain of TAPBPR form similar intramolecular disulphide bonds as those found in tapasin, and that C191 and C262 form an additional intramolecular disulphide bond (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is predicted by structural modeling and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C191 and C262 in TAPBPR form an additional intramolecular disulphide bond.
source: Our Fold and Functional Assignment System (FFAS) model of TAPBPR (Hermann et al., 2013) now supported by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data (Morozov et al., 2016), predicts that C18 and C101 in the N-terminal domain and C300 and C361 in the IgC domain of TAPBPR form similar intramolecular disulphide bonds as those found in tapasin, and that C191 and C262 form an additional intramolecular disulphide bond (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is predicted by structural modeling and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C94 in TAPBPR is very unlikely to be involved in an intramolecular disulphide bond.
source: This analysis predicts that C94 in TAPBPR is very unlikely to be involved in an intramolecular disulphide bond (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is predicted by structural modeling shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutation of C300 or C361 in the IgC domain led to significantly reduced steady-state expression of TAPBPR.
source: Mutation of C300 or C361 in the IgC domain led to significantly reduced steady-state expression of TAPBPR (Figure 2D), suggesting that these cysteines are essential for TAPBPR stability.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C300 and C361 are essential for TAPBPR stability.
source: Mutation of C300 or C361 in the IgC domain led to significantly reduced steady-state expression of TAPBPR (Figure 2D), suggesting that these cysteines are essential for TAPBPR stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced expression of mutants shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Under non-reducing conditions, TAPBPRC18A and TAPBPRC101A exhibited lower electrophoretic mobility relative to TAPBPRWT.
source: Under non-reducing conditions, TAPBPRC18A and TAPBPRC101A exhibited lower electrophoretic mobility relative to TAPBPRWT (Figure 2D), suggesting that a disulphide bond exists between C18 and C101 that is important for the structural integrity of the N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A disulphide bond exists between C18 and C101 that is important for the structural integrity of the N-terminal domain of TAPBPR.
source: Under non-reducing conditions, TAPBPRC18A and TAPBPRC101A exhibited lower electrophoretic mobility relative to TAPBPRWT (Figure 2D), suggesting that a disulphide bond exists between C18 and C101 that is important for the structural integrity of the N-terminal domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered mobility of mutants shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutation of C94 in TAPBPR did not affect steady-state protein expression or electrophoretic mobility.
source: In contrast, mutation of C94 in TAPBPR did not affect steady-state protein expression or electrophoretic mobility (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TAPBPRC94A was efficiently expressed and purified using Ni affinity and size exclusion chromatography.
source: As an additional check to determine whether TAPBPRC94A was stable and folded, this mutant was cloned into the pHLsec expression vector and transiently transfected into HEK293F cells. As observed with TAPBPRWT (Figure 2E) (Hermann et al., 2015), TAPBPRC94A was efficiently expressed and purified using Ni affinity and size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by chromatography data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The melting temperature of purified TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were the same.
source: Using differential scanning fluorimetry, the melting temperature of purified TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were the same, demonstrating that mutation of C94 to alanine did not affect protein stability (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by differential scanning fluorimetry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mutation of C94 to alanine did not affect TAPBPR protein stability.
source: Using differential scanning fluorimetry, the melting temperature of purified TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were the same, demonstrating that mutation of C94 to alanine did not affect protein stability (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is inferred from the equivalent melting temperatures shown in Figure 2G.

claim: TAPBPR still associated with both the MHC class I heavy chain and β2m in the absence of C94.
source: Comparison of TAPBPR immunoprecipitates from HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT and HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A by MS/MS analysis revealed that TAPBPR still associated with both the MHC class I heavy chain and β2m in the absence of C94 (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: UGT1 was absent in the HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A immunoprecipitate.
source: However, the most striking difference between the immunoprecipitates was the absence of UGT1 in the HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A sample (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: The amount of UGT1 that was co-immunoprecipitated was drastically reduced following mutation of C94.
source: These findings were confirmed by western blot analysis on TAPBPR immunoprecipitates, where the amount of UGT1 that was co-immunoprecipitated was drastically reduced following mutation of C94 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The C94 residue in TAPBPR is important for its association with UGT1.
source: These results suggest that the C94 residue in TAPBPR is important for its association with UGT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of UGT1 association in the C94A mutant.

claim: All lumenal cysteine residues are conserved in TAPBPR from different species.
source: Given that all lumenal cysteine residues are conserved in TAPBPR from different species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), it is possible that the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 is conserved from humans to fish.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The association between TAPBPR and UGT1 may be conserved from humans to fish.
source: Given that all lumenal cysteine residues are conserved in TAPBPR from different species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), it is possible that the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 is conserved from humans to fish.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conservation of cysteine residues shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no evidence of a disulphide-linked heterodimer between TAPBPR and UGT1 under non-reducing conditions.
source: Under non-reducing conditions, there was no evidence of a disulphide-linked heterodimer between TAPBPR and UGT1 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Both UGT1 and TAPBPR isolated from TAPBPR immunoprecipitates resolved at the predicted size of the monomeric proteins.
source: Both UGT1 and TAPBPR isolated from TAPBPR immunoprecipitates from HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells resolved at the predicted size of the monomeric proteins (~175 kDa for UGT1 and <52 kDa for TAPBPR) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TAPBPR does not form a disulphide-linked dimer with UGT1.
source: In addition to suggesting that TAPBPR does not form a disulphide-linked dimer with UGT1, the results also indicate that TAPBPR does not form a covalent bond with any other as-yet unidentified binding partner of measurable size in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of higher molecular weight species under non-reducing conditions.

claim: TAPBPR does not form a covalent bond with any other as-yet unidentified binding partner of measurable size in these cells.
source: In addition to suggesting that TAPBPR does not form a disulphide-linked dimer with UGT1, the results also indicate that TAPBPR does not form a covalent bond with any other as-yet unidentified binding partner of measurable size in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of higher molecular weight species under non-reducing conditions.

claim: Mutation of residues I83, E87, L90, H91, and D93 decreased the association of UGT1 with TAPBPR.
source: Based on our FFAS model of TAPBPR (Hermann et al., 2013), additional residues (I83, E87, L90, H91, and D93) predicted to form an α-helix on the surface of TAPBPR near C94 were also anticipated to contribute to the UGT1 interface. Mutation of these residues (UBS1: I83K, E87K, or UBS2: E87K, L90K, H91S, and D93R) decreased the association of UGT1 with TAPBPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The interaction of TAPBPR with UGT1 may involve an extended interface.
source: This suggests that the interaction of TAPBPR with UGT1 may involve an extended interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of multiple residue mutations on UGT1 binding.

claim: Distinct regions of TAPBPR are responsible for binding its interaction partners.
source: Our results thus far suggest that distinct regions of TAPBPR are responsible for binding its interaction partners, with residues in IgV and IgC domains being critical for binding MHC class I molecules (Hermann et al., 2013) and C94 in the N-terminal domain being important for associating with UGT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing different regions affect different interactions.

claim: Residues in IgV and IgC domains of TAPBPR are critical for binding MHC class I molecules.
source: Our results thus far suggest that distinct regions of TAPBPR are responsible for binding its interaction partners, with residues in IgV and IgC domains being critical for binding MHC class I molecules (Hermann et al., 2013) and C94 in the N-terminal domain being important for associating with UGT1.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work supported by citation.

claim: In TAPBPR immunoprecipitates from HeLaMKO cells transduced with TAPBPRTN5, the amount of UGT1 bound to TAPBPR was significantly reduced compared to cells expressing TAPBPRWT.
source: In TAPBPR immunoprecipitates from HeLaMKO cells transduced with TAPBPRTN5, which is unable to bind to MHC class I molecules (Hermann et al., 2013), the amount of UGT1 bound to TAPBPR was significantly reduced compared to cells expressing TAPBPRWT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Upon IFN-γ treatment, TAPBPRTN5 was able to interact with MHC class I molecules, albeit weakly.
source: Interestingly, upon IFN-γ treatment, which boosts MHC class I expression, TAPBPRTN5 was able to interact with MHC class I molecules, albeit weakly, and the amount of UGT1 bound to TAPBPRTN5 similarly increased (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The amount of UGT1 bound to TAPBPRTN5 increased upon IFN-γ treatment.
source: Interestingly, upon IFN-γ treatment, which boosts MHC class I expression, TAPBPRTN5 was able to interact with MHC class I molecules, albeit weakly, and the amount of UGT1 bound to TAPBPRTN5 similarly increased (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The association between TAPBPR and MHC class I is important for the maximum association of UGT1 with TAPBPR.
source: Together, these results suggest that the association between TAPBPR and MHC class I is important for the maximum association of UGT1 with TAPBPR, supporting the concept that a tri-molecular complex forms between TAPBPR, UGT1, and MHC class I.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that TAPBPR mutants unable to bind MHC class I have reduced UGT1 binding.

claim: A tri-molecular complex forms between TAPBPR, UGT1, and MHC class I.
source: Together, these results suggest that the association between TAPBPR and MHC class I is important for the maximum association of UGT1 with TAPBPR, supporting the concept that a tri-molecular complex forms between TAPBPR, UGT1, and MHC class I.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing interdependence of the three proteins for optimal complex formation.

claim: In HeLaMKO cells, a weak association between MHC class I and UGT1 was observed.
source: In HeLaMKO cells, we observed a weak association between MHC class I and UGT1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells, the association between MHC class I and UGT1 was significantly enhanced.
source: However, in HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells, this association was significantly enhanced (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No enhancement of MHC class I-UGT1 association was observed in cells expressing TAPBPRC94A or TAPBPRTN5, even in the presence of IFN-γ.
source: No such enhancement was observed in cells expressing the mutant forms TAPBPRC94A or TAPBPRTN5, even in the presence of IFN-γ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The association between MHC class I molecules and UGT1 is promoted by TAPBPR.
source: This suggests that the association between MHC class I molecules and UGT1 is promoted by TAPBPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced association in the presence of wild-type TAPBPR.

claim: UGT1 was found to associate weakly with both HC10- and W6/32-reactive MHC class I molecules in IFN-γ-treated HeLaM cells.
source: UGT1 was found to associate weakly with both HC10- and W6/32-reactive MHC class I molecules in IFN-γ-treated HeLaM cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKO cells, a significant reduction was observed between UGT1- and W6/32-reactive MHC class I molecules.
source: However, in IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKO cells, a significant reduction was observed between UGT1- and W6/32-reactive MHC class I molecules (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TAPBPR acts as a bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I heterodimers.
source: These results are consistent with TAPBPR acting as a bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I heterodimers and suggest that UGT1 recognition of MHC class I molecules can occur in a TAPBPR-independent manner (i.e. for the majority of HC10-reactive MHC class I) or in a TAPBPR-dependent manner (i.e with W6/32-reactive MHC class).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of TAPBPR knockout on different MHC class I populations.

claim: UGT1 recognition of MHC class I molecules can occur in a TAPBPR-independent manner.
source: These results are consistent with TAPBPR acting as a bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I heterodimers and suggest that UGT1 recognition of MHC class I molecules can occur in a TAPBPR-independent manner (i.e. for the majority of HC10-reactive MHC class I) or in a TAPBPR-dependent manner (i.e with W6/32-reactive MHC class).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some MHC class I-UGT1 association persists in TAPBPR knockout cells.

claim: UGT1 recognition of MHC class I molecules can occur in a TAPBPR-dependent manner.
source: These results are consistent with TAPBPR acting as a bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I heterodimers and suggest that UGT1 recognition of MHC class I molecules can occur in a TAPBPR-independent manner (i.e. for the majority of HC10-reactive MHC class I) or in a TAPBPR-dependent manner (i.e with W6/32-reactive MHC class).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced association of W6/32-reactive MHC class I with UGT1 in TAPBPR knockout cells.

claim: TAPBPRC94A and TAPBPRWT have comparable ability to enhance peptide dissociation and association on HLA-A*02:01 in vitro.
source: Using fluorescence polarisation, we observed a comparable ability of TAPBPRC94A and TAPBPRWT to enhance peptide dissociation and association on HLA-A*02:01 in vitro (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: In the presence of TAPBPRC94A, NLVPMVATV became a poorer competitor, as observed with TAPBPRWT.
source: Furthermore, when we tested the ability of TAPBPRC94A to discriminate between high-affinity (the labelled peptide FLPSDC*FPSV) and lower-affinity (NLVPMVATV) peptides for binding to HLA-A*02:01 (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for a comparison of the affinity of these two peptides for HLA-A2), in the presence of TAPBPRC94A, NLVPMVATV became a poorer competitor, as observed with TAPBPRWT (Figure 4C) (Hermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The peptide-editing function of TAPBPR is not altered as a direct consequence of mutation of the C94 residue.
source: These results suggest that the peptide-editing function of TAPBPR is not altered as a direct consequence of mutation of the C94 residue.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable peptide editing activity of TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A in vitro.

claim: Both TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A downregulated total MHC class I, as detected by W6/32, to a similar extent.
source: When we compared the surface expression of MHC class I molecules on HeLaMKO cells reconstituted with TAPBPRC94A or TAPBPRWT, we found that both molecules downregulated total MHC class I, as detected by W6/32, to a similar extent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Slightly lower surface expression of HLA-A*68:02 was observed in cells expressing TAPBPRC94A compared to TAPBPRWT.
source: However, we observed slightly lower surface expression of HLA-A*68:02 in cells expressing TAPBPRC94A compared to TAPBPRWT (Figure 5A and B) despite comparable levels of steady-state expression of TAPBPR in cell lines transduced with TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: A total of 690 peptides were shared between HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT and HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells.
source: A total of 690 peptides were shared between these two cell lines, while 500 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells and 174 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 500 peptides were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells.
source: A total of 690 peptides were shared between these two cell lines, while 500 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells and 174 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 174 peptides were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells.
source: A total of 690 peptides were shared between these two cell lines, while 500 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells and 174 were unique to HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a decrease in the canonical anchor residues in the peptides uniquely isolated from the TAPBPRC94A-expressing cells for HLA-A*68:02.
source: Comparison of the anchor residues found at the P2 and C-terminal (PΩ) positions of the peptides unique to TAPBPRWTcells (presumably peptides selected by the TAPBPR:UGT1 complex) with peptides unique to TAPBPRC94Acells (presumably peptides restricted by the TAPBPR:UGT1 complex) revealed a decrease in the canonical anchor residues in the peptides uniquely isolated from the TAPBPRC94A-expressing cells for HLA-A*68:02 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For HLA-B*15:03, no decrease in the prevalence of anchor residues was observed.
source: For HLA-B*15:03, no decrease in the prevalence of anchor residues was observed (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ability of TAPBPR to improve peptide optimisation on MHC class I molecules within a cellular environment can be strongly influenced by its association with UGT1, as observed for HLA-A*68:02.
source: These results suggest that the ability of TAPBPR to improve peptide optimisation on MHC class I molecules within a cellular environment can be strongly influenced by its association with UGT1, as observed here for HLA-A*68:02.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in peptide repertoire between TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A expressing cells.

claim: On HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells, only a slight increase in HLA-A68 expression was observed upon incubation at 26°C with exogenous peptide compared to cells incubated at 37°C without peptide.
source: On HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells, only a slight increase in HLA-A68 expression was observed upon incubation at 26°C with exogenous peptide compared to cells incubated at 37°C without peptide (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: On HeLaM-TAPBPRC94A cells, a significant increase in HLA-A68 expression was observed on cells incubated at 26°C with exogenous peptide compared to 37°C without peptide.
source: In contrast, on HeLaM-TAPBPRC94A cells, a significant increase in HLA-A68 expression was observed on cells incubated at 26°C with exogenous peptide compared to 37°C without peptide (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: In shUGT1-depleted HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells, a significant reduction in the association between TAPBPRWT and UGT1 was observed.
source: To further confirm that the increased expression of peptide-receptive HLA-A68 at the cell surface was a direct consequence of the loss of the association between TAPBPR and UGT1, as opposed to any other consequential effect of mutation of the C94 residue of TAPBPR, we depleted UGT1 in HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells. In shUGT1-depleted cells, a significant, although not complete, reduction in the association between TAPBPRWT and UGT1 was observed, and the strong association between TAPBPR and MHC class I was maintained (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The surface phenotype of HLA-A68 molecules in shUGT1-depleted HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells resembled that of HeLaM-TAPBPRC94A cells.
source: However, the surface phenotype of HLA-A68 molecules now resembled that of HeLaM-TAPBPRC94A cells rather than that of HeLaM-TAPBPRWT cells, with increased levels of peptide-receptive HLA-A68 that were stabilised upon incubation at 26°C with high-affinity peptide (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: The loss of the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 reduces the quality control exerted on HLA-A68.
source: Together, these results suggest that the loss of the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 reduces the quality control exerted on HLA-A68.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased peptide-receptive HLA-A68 on the surface of cells lacking TAPBPR-UGT1 association.

claim: In IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells, a substantial increase in the amount of MHC class I molecules recognised by GST-hCRTWT was observed compared to IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKO cells.
source: In IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells, a substantial increase in the amount of MHC class I molecules recognised by GST-hCRTWT was observed compared to IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKO cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells, the amount of MHC class I molecules detected by GST-hCRTWT was not increased and was comparable to that of HeLaMKO cells.
source: In IFN-γ-treated HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A cells, the amount of MHC class I molecules detected by GST-hCRTWT was not increased and was comparable to that of HeLaMKO cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No association of GST-hCRTY92A with MHC class I was observed in any of the cell lysates.
source: No association of GST-hCRTY92A with MHC class I was observed in any of the cell lysates, confirming the glycan specificity of the interactions observed with GST-hCRTWT (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The UGT1 bound to TAPBPRWT is capable of reglucosylating the N-linked glycan on MHC class I molecules, regenerating the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety.
source: These results suggest that the UGT1 bound to TAPBPRWT is capable of reglucosylating the N-linked glycan on MHC class I molecules, regenerating the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety, which can consequently be recognised by calreticulin.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased calreticulin binding to MHC class I in cells expressing TAPBPRWT.

claim: Glucosylation of the N-linked glycan was preferentially increased on HLA-A*68:02 over HLA-B*15:03 in cells expressing TAPBPRWT.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a difference in the regeneration of Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 on the HLA-A and -B molecules by the TAPBPR:UGT1 complex, finding that glucosylation of the N-linked glycan was preferentially increased on the lower MHC class I HC band (i.e. HLA-A*68:02) over the upper MHC class I HC band (i.e. HLA-B*15:03) in cells expressing TAPBPRWT (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TAPBPR exhibits prolonged association and a higher affinity for HLA-A molecules.
source: This is in keeping with previous findings that TAPBPR exhibits prolonged association and a higher affinity for HLA-A molecules (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In IFN-γ-induced HeLaM cells, the HLA-A68 HC band made up the majority of the MHC class I molecules recognised by calreticulin.
source: In IFN-γ-induced HeLaM cells, the HLA-A68 HC band made up the majority of the MHC class I molecules recognised by calreticulin (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In IFN-γ-induced HeLaMKO cells, the amount of HLA-A68 recognised by calreticulin was reduced, and proportionally more HLA-B15 had the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety attached.
source: In contrast, in IFN-γ-induced HeLaMKO cells, the amount of HLA-A68 recognised by calreticulin was reduced, and proportionally more HLA-B15 had the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 moiety attached (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by calreticulin pulldown data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Endogenous TAPBPR plays a role in modifying the glycan on MHC class I molecules.
source: These findings confirm the role of endogenous TAPBPR in modifying the glycan on MHC class I molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in glycan modification between wild-type and TAPBPR knockout cells.

claim: In HeLaMKO cells reconstituted with TAPBPRWT, an increase in the amount of MHC class I molecules bound to both tapasin and TAP was observed compared to HeLaMKO cells or cells reconstituted with TAPBPRC94A.
source: In HeLaMKO cells reconstituted with TAPBPRWT, we observed an increase in the amount of MHC class I molecules bound to both tapasin and TAP as compared to HeLaMKOcells or cells reconstituted with TAPBPRC94A (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Enhanced peptide-loading complex association with HLA-A*68:02 was specifically observed in HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells.
source: In accordance with the results observed above with the calreticulin pulldowns, we specifically observed enhanced PLC association with the lower MHC class I heavy chain band (i.e. HLA-A*68:02) in HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The increased association of HLA-A68 with tapasin in the presence of TAPBPRWT compared to TAPBPRC94A was independently verified via quantitative analysis.
source: The increased association of HLA-A68 with tapasin in the presence of TAPBPRWT compared to TAPBPRC94A was independently verified via quantitative analysis (Figure 6C), which also confirmed that the amounts of MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were similar (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The amounts of MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were similar.
source: The increased association of HLA-A68 with tapasin in the presence of TAPBPRWT compared to TAPBPRC94A was independently verified via quantitative analysis (Figure 6C), which also confirmed that the amounts of MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRC94A were similar (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells depleted of UGT1, the amount of HLA-A68 bound to tapasin and TAP was significantly reduced compared to its UGT1-competent counterpart.
source: In HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT cells depleted of UGT1, the amount of HLA-A68 bound to tapasin and TAP was significantly reduced compared to its UGT1-competent counterpart HeLaMKOTAPBPRWT, and was now comparable to HeLaMKOTAPBPRC94A without UGT1 depletion (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In addition to functioning as an MHC class I peptide editor in its own right, TAPBPR can also influence peptide selection on MHC class I molecules by promoting their association with the peptide-loading complex.
source: These results suggest that in addition to functioning as an MHC class I peptide editor in its own right, TAPBPR can also influence peptide selection on MHC class I molecules by promoting their association with the PLC, an effect that is dependent on its interaction with UGT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that TAPBPR-UGT1 interaction enhances MHC class I association with the PLC.

claim: The effect of TAPBPR on promoting MHC class I association with the peptide-loading complex is dependent on its interaction with UGT1.
source: These results suggest that in addition to functioning as an MHC class I peptide editor in its own right, TAPBPR can also influence peptide selection on MHC class I molecules by promoting their association with the PLC, an effect that is dependent on its interaction with UGT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of this effect in TAPBPRC94A mutant or UGT1-depleted cells.

claim: TAPBPR and tapasin do not appear to be functional equivalents in regard to their influence on peptide selection within a cellular environment.
source: However, within a cellular environment, the two related MHC class I chaperones do not appear to be functional equivalents in regard to their influence on peptide selection.
evidence: This is based on the authors' interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: Tapasin influences both the loading and optimisation of cargo on MHC class I molecules.
source: While tapasin influences both the loading and optimisation of cargo on MHC class I molecules, TAPBPR appears to have a more subtle, fine-tuning effect on the final peptide repertoire displayed, at least in the limited number of cell lines tested to date.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on previous studies.

claim: TAPBPR appears to have a more subtle, fine-tuning effect on the final peptide repertoire displayed.
source: While tapasin influences both the loading and optimisation of cargo on MHC class I molecules, TAPBPR appears to have a more subtle, fine-tuning effect on the final peptide repertoire displayed, at least in the limited number of cell lines tested to date.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work and observations.

claim: UGT1 provides a unique level of quality control in the MHC class I presentation pathway, acting as a sensor for the quality of the MHC class I-associated peptide cargo.
source: These studies demonstrate that UGT1 provides a unique level of quality control in the MHC class I presentation pathway, acting as a sensor for the quality of the MHC class I-associated peptide cargo (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: UGT1 can recognise a population of MHC class I molecules in a TAPBPR-independent manner.
source: Our findings here suggest that as well as UGT1 recognising a population of MHC class I molecules in a TAPBPR-independent manner, it can also recognise MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some MHC class I-UGT1 association persists in the absence of TAPBPR.

claim: UGT1 can recognise MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR.
source: Our findings here suggest that as well as UGT1 recognising a population of MHC class I molecules in a TAPBPR-independent manner, it can also recognise MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR.
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data showing TAPBPR, UGT1, and MHC class I together.

claim: TAPBPR acts as a platform or bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I.
source: In this scenario, TAPBPR most likely acts as a platform or bridge between UGT1 and MHC class I.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that TAPBPR promotes the association between UGT1 and MHC class I.

claim: The MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state.
source: As the MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state (Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016), we propose that TAPBPR permits UGT1 to reglucosylate empty or suboptimally loaded MHC class I molecules, thus providing an important quality control checkpoint in the antigen presentation pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TAPBPR permits UGT1 to reglucosylate empty or suboptimally loaded MHC class I molecules, thus providing an important quality control checkpoint in the antigen presentation pathway.
source: As the MHC class I molecules bound to TAPBPR are in a peptide-receptive state (Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016), we propose that TAPBPR permits UGT1 to reglucosylate empty or suboptimally loaded MHC class I molecules, thus providing an important quality control checkpoint in the antigen presentation pathway.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed model based on their experimental findings.

claim: UGT1 may sense different conformational perturbations in MHC class I molecules when functioning in a TAPBPR-dependent versus a TAPBPR-independent manner.
source: It is possible that UGT1 senses different conformational perturbations in MHC class I molecules when functioning in a TAPBPR-dependent versus a TAPBPR-independent manner.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of UGT1 function.

claim: The association between TAPBPR and UGT1 may be dependent on a post-translational modification of C94, such as S-nitrosylation.
source: Alternatively, the association between TAPBPR and UGT1 may be dependent on a post-translational modification of C94, such as S-nitrosylation (Hess et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of TAPBPR-UGT1 interaction.

claim: TAPBPR expression slows down the ER export of MHC class I molecules and enhances their association with tapasin.
source: Our findings here also help to further explain why TAPBPR expression slows down the ER export of MHC class I molecules and enhances their association with tapasin; findings that earlier led us to speculate that TAPBPR was a second quality control checkpoint in the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work supported by citations.

claim: TAPBPR is a second quality control checkpoint in the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway.
source: Our findings here also help to further explain why TAPBPR expression slows down the ER export of MHC class I molecules and enhances their association with tapasin; findings that earlier led us to speculate that TAPBPR was a second quality control checkpoint in the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their findings.

claim: UGT1 is not required for TAPBPR to function as an MHC class I peptide editor.
source: Although UGT1 is not required for TAPBPR to function as an MHC class I peptide editor, the TAPBPR:UGT1 complex is clearly important for MHC class I peptide optimisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro peptide editing activity of TAPBPRC94A.

claim: The TAPBPR:UGT1 complex is important for MHC class I peptide optimisation.
source: Although UGT1 is not required for TAPBPR to function as an MHC class I peptide editor, the TAPBPR:UGT1 complex is clearly important for MHC class I peptide optimisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in peptide repertoire and quality control in cells expressing TAPBPRWT versus TAPBPRC94A.

claim: TAPBPR and UGT1 work together to provide a novel quality control checkpoint in the antigen presentation pathway that influences the final peptide repertoire displayed.
source: These results demonstrate that TAPBPR and UGT1 work together to provide a novel quality control checkpoint in the antigen presentation pathway that influences the final peptide repertoire displayed.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on their experimental findings.

claim: In the peptide-loading complex, MHC class I molecules are loaded with peptides of relatively optimal affinity via tapasin.
source: We propose the following working model (Figure 7): in the PLC, MHC class I molecules are loaded with peptides of relatively optimal affinity via tapasin (step 1).
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model shown in Figure 7.

claim: Some MHC class I molecules can self-assemble with peptides in a tapasin-independent manner, resulting in complexes associated with cargoes of variable quality.
source: However, some MHC class I molecules can also self-assemble with peptides in a tapasin-independent manner, resulting in complexes associated with cargoes of variable quality (step 2).
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model shown in Figure 7.

claim: MHC class I molecules loaded with high-affinity peptides transit through the TAPBPR-mediated quality control checkpoint quickly.
source: MHC class I molecules loaded with high-affinity peptides transit through quickly.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model.

claim: MHC class I molecules associated with cargoes of low or medium affinity are captured by TAPBPR for a subsequent editing step that favours peptide dissociation.
source: However, MHC class I molecules associated with cargoes of low or medium affinity are captured by TAPBPR for a subsequent editing step that favours peptide dissociation.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model.

claim: The resultant MHC class I molecule that is devoid of peptide is reglucosylated by UGT1 associated with TAPBPR.
source: The resultant MHC class I molecule that is devoid of peptide is now reglucosylated by UGT1 associated with TAPBPR (step 6); a modification that sends the MHC class I molecule back into the calnexin/calreticulin pathway, and consequently back to the PLC (step 1) for another attempt at peptide loading.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model.

claim: Reglucosylation by UGT1 sends the MHC class I molecule back into the calnexin/calreticulin pathway, and consequently back to the peptide-loading complex for another attempt at peptide loading.
source: The resultant MHC class I molecule that is devoid of peptide is now reglucosylated by UGT1 associated with TAPBPR (step 6); a modification that sends the MHC class I molecule back into the calnexin/calreticulin pathway, and consequently back to the PLC (step 1) for another attempt at peptide loading.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed model.

claim: TAPBPR may favour binding to molecules that are initially associated with peptide in a tapasin-independent manner.
source: While the reason for TAPBPR preferentially mediating reglucosylation of HLA-A68 over HLA-B15 in HeLaM cells is currently unexplained, it is tempting to speculate that TAPBPR may favour binding to molecules that are initially associated with peptide in a tapasin-independent manner, as has been observed for many HLA-A allomorphs (Greenwood et al., 1994), and may be due to the lower affinities of their cargoes.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of TAPBPR selectivity.

claim: The unpaired cysteine residues in both tapasin and TAPBPR in mammals have evolved to perform roles that prevent the release of MHC class I molecules loaded with unsuitable peptides.
source: Thus, the unpaired cysteine residues in both tapasin and TAPBPR in mammals have evolved to perform roles that prevent the release of MHC class I molecules loaded with unsuitable peptides.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on their findings.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR have evolved to uniquely shape the peptides bound to MHC class I molecules in distinct yet intertwined ways that ultimately determine the final peptide repertoire presented on the surface of cells.
source: As a result of functioning as peptide exchange catalysts within distinct cellular environments and their unique association partners, it is becoming evident that tapasin and TAPBPR have evolved to uniquely shape the peptides bound to MHC class I molecules in distinct yet intertwined ways that ultimately determine the final peptide repertoire presented on the surface of cells.
evidence: This is the authors' overall conclusion based on their findings.
